newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Surging Budapest bourse outperforms C.Euro markets.
newsitem.headline: Surging Budapest bourse outperforms C.Euro markets.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange maintained its record-breaking form this week, hitting new record highs on the basis of new capital inflows and strong earnings.
Bourses in Prague, Warsaw and Bratislava posted mild gains, while Zagreb surprised the market with a rally. Shares in Ljubljana and Bucharest drifted lower in the summer doldrums.
The Central European Share Index (CESI) which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Czech, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian shares, firmed over two percent.
BUDAPEST

The Hungarian share market finished at a seventh successive closing high on Thursday, receiving fresh impetus from a batch of first half corporate earnings from pharmaceuticals Richter, chemicals TVK and BorsodChem.

Nigel Rendell, Emerging European Strategist at HSBC James Capel in London said the market had more room to rise, mainly because there is little else to buy in eastern Europe, with investors recently selling stocks in Poland and Czech Republic.
"I can't see either of those two countries coming back into favour, particularly in the short-term, and as a result the Hungarian market is still going to do relatively well," he said.
"It's difficult, though, to try to justify this kind of level of the index, or this kind of rally in terms of the fundamentals, in terms of valuation," Rendell added.
PRAGUE
Czech equity trading was dominated by the release of mixed first half 1997 results from the leading issues which left the PX50 index little changed.

The index's most heavily capitalised share, SPT Telecom provided the most positive news with revenues rising 25 percent. SPT which had already posted solid gains last week, in anticipation of good results, rose another five percent.
The picture was somewhat different among the leading banking issues, Komercni Banka, Ceska Sporitelna and IPB Bank, which all saw profits fall sharply.
Banks all blamed the declining performance of the Czech economy generally and the knock-on effect of the crisis in the Czech crown in particular as reasons for their slump in profits.
WARSAW

Polish shares rose 0.8 percent this week to 15,166.7 points but analysts said the stronger selling after price-fixing on Thursday suggested the market was returning to its downtrend in the run-up to September's parliamentary vote.

"It seems there's no big chance for sharp falls -- 15,000 points has already been tested and held to a degree -- so in the mid-term the bourse could hover around that line," said Dariusz Szepieniec, an analyst at Bank Slaski brokerage.
Analysts also said the central bank president's statement in a newspaper on Wednesday that she would soon raise nominal interest rates should limit buying.
On Thursday the daily Gazeta Wyborcza quoted unofficial sources as saying the central bank would raise nominal rates on Friday but the bank's press office had no comment.

Analysts also said recent flooding, seen costing billions of dollars, would dampen buying, although the finance minister said on Wednesday it was unlikely to significantly slow economic growth or create strong inflationary pressure.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) showed the signs of recovering this week, after a month of bearish mood, though the volumes traded on the main floor lagged behind spring levels.
Brokers said they welcomed the new division of the markets on the BSE, expected to become effective from August 1, which will separate liquid shares from untraded papers.
"If nothing else, I expect this to add transparency to the market, which might encourage some investors to return to Bratislava again," Dusan Sykora of ING Barings said.
However, traders said major improvement in trading activity could only be expected after the end of liquidity shortage on the local money market, which pushed interbank rates up.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks forged ahead on Thursday after breaking historic highs during the week in a surprise summer rally and traders said they saw no end to the bull run.
Traders ascribed the strong rallies on the tiny Zagreb bourse to the arrival of new foreign banks in Croatia, which brought their investors along.
Drugs concern Pliva, Zagrebacka Banka and Brewery Karlovacka Pivovara, majority owned by Chile's brewer Cervecerias Unidas, hit all-time peaks.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell one percent in lower turnover this week with market participants attributing the fall in turnover to a summer standstill.
They expected the index to keep fairly steady over the next week, while it was seen rising significantly in September when foreign and domestic demand was expected to increase.
BUCHAREST
The Bucharest bourse retreated slightly on Thursday after more than a week of bearish trend, with the three independent indices inching up amid higher demand for some listings.
Brokers said the market was unlikely to return soon to a bullish phase due to lack of buyers in the summer doldrums. Most of them expect a pick up in bourse activity in September.
